ui.aboutText: Ten chapters, in order of how important they are for everyday life and for exams (priority 1 = most important). Each chapter has rules, tables, examples and exercises. The answers are at the end of the book. The book teaches standard Italian, the Italian you hear and read all over Italy; where people say something differently in the north or the south, it says so.

k1-intro.text: Italian has two verbs that you can translate as “to be”: *essere* and *stare*. *Essere* is the main one: you use it to say who you are, where you are from, what you do, where something is and what it is like. *Stare* is mostly for how you are (*Sto bene*) and for staying in a place (*Sto a casa*). Almost every first conversation uses them.

k1-why.text: English has one verb, so the choice is new to you. For A1 it is easy: say *Sono…* for identity, origin, job, place and description, and say *Come stai? Sto bene.* for health and mood. Careful: your age, hunger and thirst use *avere*, not *essere* (*Ho trent'anni*, chapter 5).
k1-why.title: Why is this so important?

k1-h1.text: Subject pronouns and the two verbs

k1-rule1.text: The verb ending already shows the person, so Italian usually drops the pronoun: *Sono Marta. Sto bene.* Use the pronoun for contrast or to be clear: *Io sono di Napoli e lei è di Bari.* There is no word for “it”: *È grande.* *Lei* with a capital L is also the polite “you” for one person.

k1-m1.text: *Tu* is for friends, family, children and people of your age, often also with colleagues. *Lei* is for adults you don't know, for officials and for older people: at the Questura, at the Comune or at the doctor's, start with *Lei*. It takes the same verb form as *lei* (“she”): *Lei è la dottoressa Rossi?* To change over, people ask *Possiamo darci del tu?* (Can we use *tu*?).

being busy with something right now (chapter 7)

k1-m2.text: A plain job needs no article after *essere*: *Sono infermiera.* With an adjective or a description, use one: *Sono un'infermiera molto brava.* Your age goes with *avere*, not *essere*: *Ho 31 anni.*

k1-err.text: To say how you are doing, use *stare*. *Come sei?* with *essere* asks what you are like.

k2-intro.text: Almost every Italian verb ends in *-are*, *-ere* or *-ire* in the dictionary. This ending is the infinitive. To say who does something, you cut it off and add a new ending. The present tense says what happens now, what happens often and what is planned: *Lavoro a Torino. Domani parto.*

k2-why.text: You need the present tense in every conversation, and the endings do the work of the pronoun. Once you know the three groups, you can form hundreds of verbs. There is one thing to remember about *-ire*: some verbs add *-isc-* in most forms (*finisco*).
k2-why.title: Why is this so important?

k2-rule1.text: *Parlare* is a verb in *-are*, *scrivere* in *-ere*, *dormire* and *finire* in *-ire*. The *-ire* verbs come in two types. *Dormire, partire, sentire, aprire* take the plain endings. *Finire, capire, preferire, pulire* add *-isc-* in *io, tu, lui/lei* and *loro*, but not in *noi* and *voi*: *capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono*. The dictionary does not tell you which type a verb is; you learn it with the verb.

k2-m1.text: The stress stays on the same syllable in *parlo, parli, parla, parlano* but moves in *parliamo* and *parlate*. In *noi* the ending is always *-iamo* (*parliamo, scriviamo, dormiamo*). Say it aloud a few times: it is the form you will need most.

head: Verb type
Rule
Example

drop the i before another i

k2-m2.text: Italian has only one present tense for “I work” and “I am working”: *Lavoro* covers both. For something that is happening just now, you can say *Sto lavorando* (chapter 7), but you don't have to. Also, *da* tells how long something has lasted: *Abito qui da tre anni.* (= I have lived here for three years.)

k2-err.text: In a sentence with a subject, never use the infinitive. Take off *-are* and add the ending for the person.

k3-intro.text: Asking questions and saying “no” are the first tools of every conversation: at the Comune, at the pharmacy, with the landlord. Italian makes both easy. A yes/no question has the same word order as a statement, only the voice goes up. To make a sentence negative, you put *non* in front of the verb.

k3-why.text: You will ask for information every day: *Dov'è la fermata? Quanto costa? A che ora apre l'ufficio?* If you also know *non*, you can say what you don't understand, don't have or don't want. Learners often use the English word order; in Italian it is simpler.
k3-why.title: Why is this so important?

k3-rule1.text: There is no little helper verb and no inversion. *Parli italiano.* is a statement, *Parli italiano?* is a question: in writing you see the question mark, in speech the voice rises at the end. If you want to ask for a name or a person, you can put the subject at the end: *Parla italiano, Lei?* The answer starts with *sì* or *no*: *Sì, parlo italiano. – No, non parlo italiano.*

k3-m1.text: *Perché* means both “why” and “because”: *Perché studi italiano? – Perché vivo in Italia.* *Quanto* is an adjective when a noun follows, and then it agrees: *quanti figli, quante ore*. *Come* and *dove* lose the last vowel before *è*: *Com'è? Dov'è?* The question word comes first: *Dove abiti?* (not *Dove tu abiti?*). Ask about time with *A che ora…?*: *A che ora apre l'ufficio?*

k3-rule2.text: *Non* goes directly before the verb: *Non capisco. Non lavoro il sabato.* Object pronouns stay between *non* and the verb: *Non lo so.* After *non* you can add *mai* (never), *niente* (nothing), *nessuno* (nobody). In Italian these words come after the verb *and* you still need *non*: *Non vedo mai nessuno.* There is no “double negative” problem. If *nessuno* or *niente* comes first, you leave out *non*: *Nessuno parla.*

k3-err.text: *Non* stands directly before the verb. It never goes after the verb and never at the end.

k4-intro.text: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, and it comes with a small word in front of it, the article: *il libro, la casa*. The article, the noun and the adjective all agree in gender and number. It sounds like a lot, but a few rules cover most words. This chapter also teaches *c'è* and *ci sono* (there is, there are).

k4-why.text: Gender and articles are in every sentence. If you learn each noun with its article (*il lavoro, la residenza*), you learn the gender for free. And *c'è / ci sono* is the way to ask about things everywhere: *C'è il riscaldamento? Ci sono i mezzi pubblici?*
k4-why.title: Why is this so important?

k4-rule1.text: Most nouns in *-o* are masculine (*il libro*) and most in *-a* are feminine (*la casa*). Nouns in *-e* can be either: *il nome, la notte*; learn them with the article. People who can be either sex have one form for both: *il / la collega, il / la turista, il / la cantante*. Some words in *-a* are masculine: *il problema, il programma, il sistema, il tema*. A few in *-o* are feminine: *la mano, la radio, la foto*.

the (singular)
the (plural)

k4-m1.text: The article depends on the sound at the start of the next word: *il bravo studente* but *lo studente bravo*. A feminine word always takes *una*, or *un'* before a vowel: *un'amica*, never *un amica*. Also learn that Italian uses the article more than English: *Mi piace il caffè. Il lunedì lavoro. La signora Rossi è qui.*

k4-rule2.text: An adjective agrees with its noun. The adjectives in *-o* have four forms; those in *-e* have two. Most adjectives come after the noun: *una casa grande, un lavoro difficile*. A few common short ones often come before: *un bel posto, una buona idea, un nuovo lavoro*.

k4-rule3.text: Use *c'è* for one thing and *ci sono* for more than one: *C'è un supermercato qui vicino. Ci sono due camere e un bagno.* The question has the same words: *C'è una farmacia? Ci sono i mezzi pubblici?* In the negative: *Non c'è l'ascensore. Non ci sono problemi.* To say where something is, use *essere* (*Dov'è la farmacia? È in via Roma.*) and to point to something, use *ecco*: *Ecco il bus!*

k4-err.text: *Problema* ends in *-a*, but it is masculine. Words from Greek in *-ma* (*il programma, il sistema, il tema*) are masculine.

k5-intro.text: Some of the most common Italian verbs do not follow the normal endings: *avere, andare, fare, venire, dare, uscire, dire, bere, sapere*. You must learn their forms by heart. The good news is that the endings for *noi* and *voi* are almost always regular, and the third person plural often looks like *io* plus *-no* (*vado → vanno*, *faccio → fanno*).

k5-why.text: These verbs are in almost every conversation: *Che cosa fai? Vado al lavoro. Ho un appuntamento. Non lo so.* Learn them first and you can say a lot with very few words.
k5-why.title: Why is this so important?

k5-m1.text: In the written forms of *avere*, *ho, hai, ha, hanno* start with a silent *h*: it only separates them from other words (*ho / o*, *hai / ai*, *ha / a*, *hanno / anno*). *Dà* (he gives) has an accent so that it is not confused with *da* (from, by). Remember *sapere* and *conoscere*: *Sai l'inglese? Conosci Marco?*

k5-h3.text: andare, venire and the little words a, in, da

head: Where to
Preposition
Example
cells: a country, a region, many buildings

k5-rule1.text: *Andare* goes away from the speaker, *venire* comes towards the speaker or the person we talk to: *Vengo da te alle otto.* (I'm coming to your place at eight.) *Stasera esco con gli amici. Vieni anche tu?* *Fare* is used in many fixed phrases: *fare la spesa, fare colazione, fare una domanda, fare il medico* (to work as a doctor), *fa freddo, fa caldo*.

k5-err.text: To go to a person, use *da*. The article joins in: *da + il = dal*. Use *a* or *in* only for places.

k6-intro.text: Three small things make Italian sound Italian: *piacere* (to like), reflexive verbs (*mi alzo*, *mi chiamo*) and the little pronouns *lo, la, li, le* that stand for a thing or a person you have already named. All three put a short word *before* the verb.

k6-why.text: You say what you like or don't like every day. You also use reflexive verbs for your daily routine and your name (*Mi chiamo…*). And with the object pronouns you don't have to repeat nouns: *Il permesso? Lo ritiro in Questura.* Good Italian needs these three.
k6-why.title: Why is this so important?

k6-h1.text: Piacere: the thing is the subject

k6-rule1.text: In Italian you don't say “I like coffee”. You say “the coffee pleases me”: *Mi piace il caffè.* The thing you like is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: *piace* for one thing or for a verb, *piacciono* for more than one thing. The person is a small pronoun in front: *mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi, gli*. To stress the person, add *a me, a te…* in front.

k6-m1.text: To say “me too”, use *anche a me*; “me neither” is *neanche a me*. *Mi piace il pesce. – Anche a me.* *Non mi piace il caldo. – Neanche a me.* With a different answer, say *A me sì* or *A me no*. For a stronger feeling, use *mi piace molto* or *mi piace tanto*; to say “I love”, use *adoro* or *amo*.

k6-rule2.text: A reflexive verb has *-si* at the end of the infinitive (*alzarsi, vestirsi, chiamarsi*), and a small word before the conjugated verb: *mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si*. It is common for the daily routine: *Mi sveglio alle sei, mi alzo, mi lavo e mi vesto.* Some verbs are reflexive in Italian and not in English: *chiamarsi* (to be called), *sentirsi* (to feel), *sedersi* (to sit down).

k6-rule3.text: A direct object pronoun replaces a person or thing: *Vedo Marco → Lo vedo. Compro la pizza → La compro.* It stands directly before the verb. With a vowel it loses the vowel: *L'aiuto* (I help him / her). Pronouns for “to someone” (indirect) work in the same way: *Ti telefono. Le scrivo una lettera. Gli dico la verità.*

k6-err.text: With *piacere*, the thing is the subject. The person is the small pronoun *mi, ti…* and never *io*, *tu*.

k7-intro.text: With three very common verbs you say what you must, can and want to do: *dovere, potere, volere*. They take another verb right after them, in the infinitive: *Devo andare. Posso entrare? Voglio capire.* With *stare + gerundio* you say what you are doing at this moment: *Sto lavorando.*

k7-why.text: You need these verbs to ask for things, to make appointments and to explain what is possible: *Posso prenotare una visita? Devo rinnovare il permesso. Non posso venire domani.* They also make your Italian polite: *Può ripetere?* and *Vorrei un appuntamento.*
k7-why.title: Why is this so important?

head: Verb
Use
Example
cells: to be able to, to be allowed to, to ask politely

k7-rule1.text: The second verb is in the infinitive and comes *without* a preposition: *Devo lavorare*, not *Devo di lavorare*. To make the sentence negative, put *non* before the modal verb: *Non posso venire.* A pronoun comes before the modal verb or is attached to the infinitive. Both are right: *Lo devo fare. / Devo farlo.* To be polite, use *vorrei* (I would like): *Vorrei un appuntamento, per favore.*

k7-m1.text: Also useful: *bisogna* + infinitive says that something is necessary in general: *Bisogna prenotare.* *Ci vuole* says what it takes: *Ci vuole un'ora per arrivare.* (It takes an hour.) *Sapere* + infinitive is “know how to”: *So nuotare.* but *Posso nuotare* is “I am allowed to / I am able to now”.

k7-h2.text: Stare + gerundio: what is happening now

k7-rule2.text: Take *stare* in the right person and add the gerund of the main verb. The gerund ends in *-ando* for *-are* verbs and in *-endo* for *-ere* and *-ire* verbs: *parlare → parlando, scrivere → scrivendo, dormire → dormendo*. A few verbs are irregular: *fare → facendo, dire → dicendo, bere → bevendo*. Use it for something that is going on right now: *Che cosa stai facendo? – Sto cucinando.* Don't use it for the future: for a plan, use the present (*Domani lavoro*).

k7-m2.text: *Stare per* + infinitive says that something is about to happen: *Il treno sta per partire. Sto per uscire.* Do not mix up the three: *Sto lavorando* (right now), *Lavoro* (in general) and *Sto per lavorare* (I'm about to).

k7-err.text: *Dovere, potere* and *volere* take the infinitive directly. Don't put *di*, *a* or *per* after them.

k8-intro.text: The passato prossimo is the tense you use to say what happened: *Ieri ho lavorato. Sono arrivata nel 2019.* It has two parts: a form of *avere* or *essere*, and the participle of the main verb. Learners find the choice between *avere* and *essere* hard, but there is a clear rule.

k8-why.text: You need the past to tell your story at the doctor's, at work and at the Questura: *Sono arrivato in Italia due anni fa. Ho lavorato in un ristorante. Ho già pagato.* It is also the first tense that shows up in every A2 exam.
k8-why.title: Why is this so important?

head: Auxiliary
Which verbs
Example
cells: most verbs, and every verb with a direct object
verbs of movement and change: andare, venire, partire, arrivare, uscire, entrare, tornare, restare, nascere, diventare, essere

k8-rule1.text: With *avere* the participle never changes: *Ho mangiato. Abbiamo mangiato.* With *essere* the participle agrees with the subject in gender and number, like an adjective: *Marco è andato. Maria è andata. Siamo arrivati. Siete arrivate.* With *avere*, the participle only agrees with the pronouns *lo, la, li, le* before it: *Il documento? L'ho portato. La lettera? L'ho letta.* To make the sentence negative, put *non* before *avere* or *essere*: *Non ho capito. Non sono partita.*

k8-m1.text: Time words that go with the passato prossimo: *ieri, ieri sera, stamattina, la settimana scorsa, due anni fa, nel 2019*. Also useful: *già* (already) and *non… ancora* (not yet), placed between the two parts: *Ho già pagato. Non ho ancora ricevuto la lettera.* In speech in the south of Italy you may hear the passato remoto instead (*Ieri mangiai*); we teach the passato prossimo, which is standard everywhere and what the exams use.

k8-err.text: *Andare* is a verb of movement and takes *essere*. Think of the verbs that show where you go, come, stay, are born: *andare, venire, partire, arrivare, uscire, tornare, restare, nascere*.

k9-intro.text: Italian has two main past tenses for telling a story. The passato prossimo (chapter 8) says what happened. The *imperfetto* says what things were like, what used to happen and what was going on: *Era una bella giornata. Da bambino abitavo a Napoli.* With both together you can tell a real story.

k9-why.text: Any time you tell your story, your job, your journey or a problem, you switch between the two tenses. The imperfetto is also regular and easy to form, so it is a good investment. At B1 the exam asks you to tell a story, and you can only do it with both.
k9-why.title: Why is this so important?

k9-rule1.text: For regular verbs, take off *-re* and add *-vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano*: *parla-re → parlavo*; *scrive-re → scrivevo*; *dormi-re → dormivo*. Only a few verbs are irregular. *Essere* has its own forms (*ero, eri, era…*). *Fare, dire, bere* are based on an older stem: *facevo, dicevo, bevevo*. All the other verbs are regular.

head: Use
Example
cells: a description: weather, time, age, people
an action in progress in the background
the scene for a single event

head: Question
Tense
Example
cells: What was it like? What used to happen?

k9-m1.text: Time words that often go with the imperfetto: *di solito, sempre, spesso, ogni giorno, ogni estate, da bambino, allora, mentre*. Time words for a single event go with the passato prossimo: *ieri, un giorno, improvvisamente, poi*. Typical stories use both: *Era sera e pioveva. Sono uscita, ho preso l'autobus e sono arrivata a casa. Mia madre mi aspettava.*

k9-err.text: For something that used to happen again and again, use the imperfetto, not the passato prossimo. *Sempre, ogni giorno, di solito* are the usual clue.

k10-intro.text: At B1 you want to say more than facts: what you will do, what you would like, what depends on a condition, what you think. Four tools do that: the *futuro semplice* (*parlerò*), the *condizionale* (*parlerei*), sentences with *se* (*Se piove, resto a casa*) and the first *congiuntivo* (*Penso che sia giusto*).

k10-why.text: This is the language of plans, advice, polite requests and opinions. In a B1 exam for citizenship or work you must give your opinion and talk about your plans. The congiuntivo is what makes your Italian sound educated, and it is the first thing a teacher listens for.
k10-why.title: Why is this so important?

k10-rule1.text: Take the infinitive, drop the final *-e*, change *-are* to *-er-* and add *-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno*: *parlare → parlerò, scrivere → scriverò, dormire → dormirò*. Verbs in *-care, -gare* keep the hard sound (*cercherò, pagherò*), and in *-ciare, -giare* the *i* disappears (*comincerò, mangerò*). Use the future for plans, predictions and promises: *Domani andrò in Questura. Domenica pioverà. Ti aiuterò.* It also says what you suppose: *Saranno le otto. Sarà a casa.* For a plan that is very close, the present is more usual: *Domani parto.*

k10-m1.text: Common verbs with a short stem: *andare → andrò, venire → verrò, fare → farò, potere → potrò, dovere → dovrò, volere → vorrò, vedere → vedrò, sapere → saprò, dare → darò, stare → starò*. After *quando*, careful Italian puts the future for a future event: *Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò.* In everyday speech the present is also common (*Quando arrivo, ti chiamo*), but the future is the form exams expect.

k10-rule2.text: The condizionale uses the same stem as the futuro with the endings *-ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero*: *parlerei, andrei, potrei*. It is used for polite requests (*Potresti aiutarmi? Vorrei un caffè.*), advice (*Dovresti andare dal medico. Io, al tuo posto, aspetterei.*) and wishes (*Mi piacerebbe vivere a Roma.*).

k10-rule3.text: For something that is possible or likely, put the present after *se* and use the present, the future or the imperative in the other part: *Se piove, resto a casa. Se hai tempo, chiamami. Se arrivo tardi, ti avviso.* Careful: after *se* we normally do *not* use the future in this type of sentence. Use *quando* (not *se*) when it is sure to happen: *Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò.*

k10-rule4.text: The three singular forms are the same, so you often need the pronoun. *-are* verbs take *-i* (*parli*), *-ere* and *-ire* verbs take *-a* (*scriva, dorma*); the verbs in *-isc-* keep it (*finisca, capisca*). Irregular verbs: *fare → faccia, andare → vada, venire → venga, potere → possa, volere → voglia, dovere → debba, dire → dica, stare → stia, sapere → sappia, uscire → esca.*

head: Trigger
Example
cells: doubt: dubito che, non sono sicuro che
feeling: sono contento che, mi dispiace che
impersonal: bisogna che, è importante che

k10-m2.text: The congiuntivo comes after these triggers when the subject of the second verb is *different* from the first: *Voglio che tu venga.* If the subject is the same, use *di* or nothing and the infinitive: *Penso di avere ragione. Voglio partire.* In everyday speech many Italians use the indicative after *penso che* (*Penso che è giusto*), but it is not accepted as correct in exams and in writing: use the congiuntivo.

k10-err.text: After *penso che, credo che, voglio che, bisogna che*, the verb is in the congiuntivo. Learn the form *sia* first: it is the most frequent one.
